A1.justification: Both complete PDFs describe the same test-time training study, despite the broadened title and substantial reorganization. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison. Numerical inconsistencies can be identified directly rather than treated as missing evidence.

before.justification: v1 reports original ARC experiments, including training and inference ablations, model-size comparisons, and full public-validation results.

after.justification: v2 retains the original ARC experiments and adds original BIG-Bench Hard experiments, task-level analyses, and an ARC semi-private evaluation.

M1.justification: The core leave-one-out, LoRA, and ARC hierarchical-voting procedure remains. v2 adds an inputs-and-outputs loss variant in Section 3.2 and adapts the procedure to BBH without synthetic preliminary fine-tuning or geometric augmentation/voting. These are limited extensions; renaming E2E as Direct I/O does not itself change the method.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates ARC visual-grid reasoning only. v2 adds all 27 BIG-Bench Hard tasks across 23 task types and an ARC semi-private hidden-task evaluation, substantially expanding both task requirements and evaluation populations. The original 80 ARC development tasks are identical across versions.

E2.justification: ARC Table 1 adds reported comparisons with OpenAI o1 preview, DeepSeek r1, and OpenAI o3 while retaining the earlier comparison rows. BBH adds a zero-shot reference and new permutation/loss controls. E2E and Direct I/O are matching comparators, and the QLoRA comparison survives in Appendix C.2.

E3.justification: The new BBH evaluation introduces Llama 3.1-8B, ten demonstration examples per task with the remaining examples held out, 40 demonstration shuffles, rank-64 LoRA, and greedy decoding with custom answer extraction. Semi-private ARC testing adds an external evaluation procedure. The original ARC development set and pass@2 scoring remain.

E4.justification: Sections 5.3–5.4 and Appendix F add BBH ablations of example permutations, training losses, and adapter sharing, plus task-specific gains and failures. The semi-private ARC result adds a generalization check. Existing ARC analyses remain, including the QLoRA result moved from the main figure to Appendix C.2.

E5.justification: v1 explicitly reports no comprehensive standard-error analysis. v2 reports BBH averages over five demonstration-selection seeds, identifies seeds 42–46, and provides per-method standard errors in Table 7. This introduces substantive uncertainty reporting, although corresponding ARC uncertainty estimates remain absent and no increase in ARC run counts is established.

E6.justification: New results include BBH accuracies of 50.5% for ICL, 57.8% for TTT, and 59.8% for shared TTT, plus 47.5% on semi-private ARC. Most matched ARC results remain unchanged. Table 1 changes the ensemble entry from 61.9% to 62.8%, but v2's abstract, caption, and prose still say 61.9%, leaving that revision unresolved. Section 4.6 corrects the original prose baseline from 39.3% to 18.3%, matching both versions' tables.

T1.justification: Section 3.2 adds a mathematical definition of the inputs-and-outputs objective by adding conditional input losses to the output objective. Existing leave-one-out, augmentation, and inference mathematics is largely restated or relocated. Neither version contains a theorem or proof development.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and conclusion broaden the contribution from ARC abstract reasoning to few-shot learning across ARC and BBH, including a new claim of a 7.3-percentage-point BBH improvement. The emphasis shifts toward limitations of ICL and model adaptability. v1's overall state-of-the-art ensemble claim is dropped, while the narrower open-source neural ARC comparison remains.

C2.justification: v2 explains why shared adapters may help BBH but hurt ARC, hypothesizes benefits for structural patterns and limitations for sequential computation, and discusses the semi-private decline as possible distribution shift. It extends leakage concerns to BBH and removes v1's hardware-based submission barrier and promised future uncertainty analysis. These substantially revise applicability and limitations.

D1.justification: Appendix F adds BBH hyperparameter search spaces, training-step budgets, evaluation implementation information, libraries, and A100 runtime; a separate BBH code link is supplied. Table 6 newly identifies preferred ARC learning rates by model size. Conversely, v1's disclosure of approximately 600,000 generated fine-tuning tasks is omitted, without evidence that the underlying dataset changed.

R1.justification: v2 substantially broadens positioning through local and transductive learning, retrieval-based TTT, MetaICL, BBH, and an explicit distinction from recurrent-state interpretations of TTT. New references include Bottou and Vapnik, Joachims, Hardt and Sun, and Hübॉटter and colleagues. Earlier Krause dynamic-evaluation and Cole citations disappear; publication-metadata updates are not counted as new works.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and preliminaries are extensively rewritten. The method-centered narrative becomes general TTT design followed by separate ARC and BBH sections and related work. Fine-tuning and detailed inference material move into reorganized appendices. The title, author list, and E2E terminology also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from one to two columns, Figure 1 is redesigned, and a new design-summary diagram and BBH figures/tables are added. Existing diagrams and tables are relocated and resized; the model-size panel is separately redisplayed. QLoRA disappears from the ARC ablation chart while its numerical result remains in appendix prose.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's public-ARC-only evaluation: BBH tests applicability without ARC-specific augmentations, five-seed estimates quantify reliability, and semi-private ARC testing addresses a stated evaluation limitation. Task-specific analyses also reveal important boundaries and reversals in adapter-sharing benefits. These gains outweigh reporting defects, including the 62.8%/61.9% ensemble inconsistency and newly presenting ARC task counts as percentages. ARC uncertainty reporting remains incomplete.
